candidate.answerReason: Driving entirely in sunshine would cover 20 miles. The 4-mile shortfall, caused by a speed reduction of 10 miles per hour during rain, requires 0.4 hour, or 24 minutes.

methods.label: Compare with an entirely sunny trip
methods.explanation:
Imagine Shelby driving in sunshine for all \(40\) minutes. She would cover
\[
30\cdot\frac{40}{60}=20\text{ miles}.
\]
This is \(20-16=4\) miles more than she actually drove. Each hour driven in rain instead of sunshine reduces the distance by \(30-20=10\) miles. The entire shortfall therefore comes from \(4/10\) hour of rainy driving, which is
\[
\frac{4}{10}\cdot60=24\text{ minutes}.
\]
This leaves \(16\) minutes in sunshine. Those two parts cover \(8\) miles each, confirming the stated total distance and time. Shelby drove in the rain for \(24\) minutes, choice C.
methods.levelReason: The solution uses only speed times time, an arithmetic comparison, and conversion between hours and minutes.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is the speed-time-distance relationship for two parts of one journey. The method isolates the distance lost during rainy driving and uses the inverse multiplication relationship to find its duration. Hour-minute conversion supports the calculation. The meeting-and-catching-up node does not fit this journey.
